data.title: S&P 500 Prediction 2027: Targets From 5,000 To 8,900
data.description:
Why Are Wall Street Banks Divided on the S&P 500 Outlook 2027?

The S&P 500 outlook 2027 is becoming a major debate among institutional investors. While UBS and Goldman Sachs expect further gains, Panmure Liberum warns that higher interest rates, expensive valuations and slowing AI investment could trigger a substantial market correction.

The difference between an optimistic 8,900 target and a bearish 5,000 forecast highlights how uncertain the next phase of the US equity bull market could be.

UBS and Goldman Sachs Lead the Bullish S&P 500 Target 2027 Forecasts

UBS maintained its S&P 500 year-end forecast 2027 at 8,900 on November 10, implying approximately 17.7% upside from the November 13 closing price of 7,561.67.

UBS strategist Keith Parker expects earnings growth and a recovery in investor confidence to support equities. The bank forecasts S&P 500 earnings per share (EPS) of $430 in 2027, representing 18% growth, followed by $490 in 2028.

Meanwhile, the Goldman Sachs S&P 500 forecast 2027 places the index at 8,700 over the next 12 months, implying approximately 15.1% upside from the November 13 close.

Goldman expects US earnings growth to slow from 36% in 2026 to 11% in 2027. However, it believes improving valuations, economic growth and potentially lower borrowing costs could support further gains. he said,

"From here, we expect equities to ​generate positive returns, albeit with higher volatility than in ​recent years,"

Other institutional forecasts are similarly optimistic:

  • Barclays: 8,800 by year-end 2027.

  • Wells Fargo Investment Institute: 8,600 to 8,800 by year-end 2027.

These targets suggest that major institutions generally expect the broader US equity market to extend its advance, although their forecast periods and assumptions differ.

Panmure Liberum Warns of a Bearish 5,000 Target

Not every investment bank expects the S&P 500 to continue climbing.

Panmure Liberum research analyst Joachim Klement forecasts the index could fall to 5,000 by the end of 2027, representing approximately 33.9% downside from its November 13 close.

His bearish outlook reflects concerns about persistent inflation, elevated bond yields and the possibility that the AI investment boom could lose momentum.

The concern is particularly relevant because technology companies have contributed significantly to recent index gains.

According to Reuters report, quoted Klement:

Joachim Klement said,

"If we keep seeing higher bond yields and interest rates..."

He warned that continued monetary tightening could bring the current equity bull market closer to its end.

The bearish forecast stands in sharp contrast to UBS's 8,900 target, illustrating the uncertainty surrounding the S&P 500 prediction 2027.

S&P 500 EPS 2027 Forecast: Earnings Growth Remains Critical

Corporate earnings will be one of the biggest drivers of the S&P 500's performance in 2027.

EPS, or earnings per share, measures how much profit a company generates for each outstanding share. For the S&P 500, aggregate earnings growth helps investors assess whether higher index valuations are supported by corporate profitability.

UBS expects index EPS to reach $430 in 2027, representing 18% annual growth.

Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, expects US earnings growth to slow to 11% in 2027 from 36% in 2026.

This difference matters because slower earnings growth could limit further valuation expansion, even if companies remain profitable.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which measures how much investors pay for each dollar of earnings, also plays an important role.

UBS strategist Keith Parker noted that the S&P 500's forward P/E ratio declined approximately 20% during 2026, despite strong earnings growth.

UBS argues that this valuation adjustment could create room for further gains. However, Goldman warns that slowing AI capital expenditure could affect technology-related earnings and increase market volatility.

AI Investment and Treasury Yields Could Determine the Market Direction

Artificial intelligence investment and interest rates remain two major variables behind the competing S&P 500 year-end forecast 2027 scenarios.

Goldman Sachs expects AI capital expenditure growth to peak, potentially slowing earnings momentum among companies benefiting from data-centre and semiconductor spending.

UBS also identifies slowing AI investment and another increase in Treasury yields as major downside risks.

Higher bond yields can make equities less attractive because investors receive better returns from government securities. They can also reduce the present value of future corporate earnings, putting additional pressure on growth-stock valuations.

The US 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.143% on November 16, 2026, according to Reuters-reported market data.

Goldman Sachs Chief Global Equity Strategist Peter Oppenheimer highlighted the changing risk environment.

Oppenheimer said in Goldman's 2027 outlook, reported November 13:

"Risks are becoming more two-sided."

Technical Indicators: What the SP500 Chart Says?

The recent trading structure indicates short-term weakness, although the index remains within its broader 2026 advance. Price sits below the 20-day EMA (7,600.72, blue) and 50-day EMA (7,635.33, orange). Both averages have turned lower since the early-October peak, when the index set its 52-week high of 7,844.52.

Support is marked at 7,499.40 (November 13 low) and 7,470.43 (November 10 low). November 13’s long lower wick shows buyers stepping in near 7,500 before the close.

Why is the stock market down today?

US stocks are facing pressure from concerns about elevated Treasury yields, slowing AI investment growth, corporate earnings expectations and uncertainty surrounding Federal Reserve policy. Higher bond yields can make equities less attractive, particularly high-valuation technology stocks.

Is a recession coming in the US in 2028?

A US recession in 2028 is possible but not confirmed or inevitable. Slower corporate earnings growth, persistent inflation, higher borrowing costs and weaker consumer spending could increase recession risks. data.title: FX Daily: Higher US Real Rates Dominate
data.description:
US short-dated real interest rates are pushing back to their highest levels since 2023 as markets get the message that the Fed is ready to apply the brakes. These high real rates are sucking funds out of asset classes like precious metals and are triggering a broader fallout across emerging market currencies. There is no reason to fight this trend near term.

Higher US real rates are sucking funds into the dollar.

USD: Two-year real swap rates are now 2.4%

The market has got the message. We understand the Fed needs to take rates higher to get inflation back to target. And we are now seeing US two-year real rates (swap rates less the zero-coupon inflation swap) pushing above 2.40%. The last time rates were at this level was in 2023. Higher real rates are especially negative for zero-yielding precious metals and one of the reasons why gold and silver and linked currencies like the South African rand and Thai baht are under pressure.

On the Fed, we have seen further comments from Chris Waller alongside the release of the October FOMC minutes over the last 24 hours. Waller has now turned ultra-hawkish and is pushing for more than a reversal of the 75bp 'insurance' rate cuts seen last year. However, he may be out on his own here. According to the FOMC minutes, only a 'couple' of Fed voters favoured a faster pace of tightening at the October meeting and the market now looks quite settled on pricing 25bp hikes in December, January and next summer. When could these views be challenged? Perhaps not until energy-softened November CPI data is released on 10 December.

This all seems a very positive story for the dollar then. There has also been speculation that foreign interest in Anthropic's blockbuster IPO has seen some demand for the dollar this week. If that is the case, that dollar demand could wane into tomorrow once IPO allocations are settled. Yet there are good reasons for the dollar to be at current levels, and DXY advancing to the 104.60 area remains our bias for now.

For today, all eyes will be on how Anthropic (ANT) trades on its first day, while low initial jobless claims should point to a solid US jobs market.

EUR: Macro resilience, but swamped by the dollar

EUR/USD is consolidating under 1.10 as the strong dollar dominates across the board. EUR/USD price action masks ongoing resilience on the macro side, where business confidence remains relatively high and better-than-expected eurozone growth rates this year are projected to continue into 2027. As above, it is hard to see the strong dollar trend turning before mid-December, and we think EUR/USD still risks a drop to the 1.0880 area.

A light data calendar today just sees the release of September eurozone current account data. High energy prices in September may have weighed further on the surplus, although Germany delivered a surprisingly stronger current account surplus that month.

ZAR: SARB to leave rates on hold today

The South African Reserve Bank meets to set interest rates today. Having hiked interest rates to 7.25% in September, no one is expecting a further hike today. However, money markets do price another 25bp hike in early 2027. Unlike Banxico, the SARB has been responsive to the inflation shock and we see much greater scope for the rand to bounce back than Mexico's peso. See a more in-depth discussion on the rand's prospects in our 2027 FX Outlook.

MXN: Lack of rate protection comes home to roost

At one point, USD/MXN was nearly 3% higher on the day as large parts of the emerging market complex succumbed to the strong dollar. We heavily discussed the risk of peso underperformance in our 2027 Latam FX Outlook, given that Banxico had cut the policy rate spread protection over the Fed to very slim levels. We see no reason for USD/MXN to turn lower until the broader dollar trend turns. And, ultimately, that may not be until the second quarter of next year, when US inflation is substantially falling.

data.title: Risk Is Cheap, Safety Isn’t
data.description:
We tweeted the graphic below to show just how cheap NVDA shares have gotten compared to Walmart. While many replies agree with our view, quite a few didn’t.

Some of our critics argue that Nvidia’s earnings growth will not come close to the 65% annual pace analysts expect, making the stock far riskier than a steady, dependable defensive stock like Walmart. We agree, Nvidia may fall short of the lofty forecasts. However, the important analysis for investors is a deep dive into the combination of valuations and expectations.

The analysis we share is a valuation comparison of NVDA to WMT, not a comparison of either stock to the market or any other stock. It is incredibly instructive to show how valuations and expectations play into investment strategy.

A stock’s PEG ratio divides a company’s P/E by its expected five-year earnings growth. Using trailing P/E ratios, Walmart trades at 45 times earnings with expected growth of 11%, for a PEG of 4.09. Nvidia, at 17 times earnings with 65% expected growth, has a PEG of 0.26. For Nvidia’s PEG to equal Walmart’s, it only needs to grow earnings by about 4.2% per year over five years. That is only about 10% of current expectations and even half of Walmart’s.

Here’s another way to think about it. If Walmart shares stay the same price for five years and it achieves its expected 11% growth, its P/E falls to about 26.7. Nvidia’s P/E would also be 26.7 if its earnings declined by over 8% a year.

So yes, we are comfortable taking the “risk” that Nvidia doesn’t meet earnings growth expectations versus the “safety” of Walmart. Simply, the market is providing a lot of cushion for being wrong.

What To Watch Today

IPO

Anthropic (ANT) prices Wednesday evening and is scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market today. Proposed range: $70 to $78 per share, 825 million Class A shares. Settlement Friday, November 20.

Economy

Earnings

Fed Speakers

Hammack 8:50 a.m. · Goolsbee 12:30 p.m. · Barr 2:15 p.m. · Barkin 4:00 p.m. · Paulson 6:30 p.m. (all ET)

Market Trading Update

On Tuesday, we laid out the supply side of the Anthropic IPO and why roughly $90 billion of new stock matters more than the valuation debate. This morning, the deal goes live. Anthropic (ANT) priced last night and opens for trading on Nasdaq today. The question I’m getting most is simple. Should you buy it?

History gives a fairly blunt answer. Back in June, the Bull Bear Report warned readers to wait on the SpaceX IPO because big debuts usually sell off in the first couple of months. SpaceX (SPCX) priced at $135, jumped 19% on day one, and closed at $201.80 on June 16. By August 5, it had closed at $108.27, a 46% decline from the peak. On Monday, it finished at $137.36, barely above the offer price five months later.

That wasn’t bad luck. Such is the nature of new issues. The table below, rebuilt from Carson Investment Research, tracks 36 major IPOs since Google in 2004. The average first-day gain was 49%, and 92% closed higher on day one. The average maximum drawdown in the first 12 months was 55%, and NOT one of these companies escaped a decline of at least 13%.

The reasons are mechanical. Floats are tiny at the start, so modest buying moves the price a lot. Then supply arrives as lockups expire and insiders sell. Anthropic is selling 825 million shares, roughly 5% of its fully diluted share count, a float about the size of SpaceX’s. Sentiment is running hot, too. On Monday, a crypto contract tracking ANT on Hyperliquid traded at $98.67, and CNBC reported Tuesday that demand is likely to push prices above the $70-$78 range.

None of this says Anthropic is a bad company. It says the first few months of a “hot” IPO are usually the worst time to own it. If you want exposure, here are the rules we’d follow:

  1. Don’t buy the open. Let price discovery and the first-day pop play out.

  2. Use limit orders only. Market orders on debut day are an invitation to overpay.

  3. Start small. A starter position of 1% or less limits the damage if history repeats.

  4. Build in thirds. Add after the first earnings report, after analyst coverage begins, and after the first lockup expires.

  5. Calendar the lockups. Know when insider supply hits the market.

  6. Define the exit before the entry. Decide what price or event proves you wrong.

Our portfolios will sit out the debut. We’d rather pay a little more later with real information than pay a premium today for a story.

The pop is the marketing. The drawdown is the tuition.

Nvidia Kills It: Investors Aren’t Jumping For Joy

Nvidia delivered a near-perfect quarter, and the market responded with a rather tame golf clap. Revenue of $115.8 billion rose 103% from a year ago and beat the roughly $109 billion consensus. Further, management guided the coming quarter about $5 billion higher than prior expectations, and the board added $150 billion to the buyback authorization. Shares opened Wednesday morning about 3% higher but turned negative within the first hour of trading, as we share below. Not what one would expect given the excellent results.

Investors have ample reason to be reserved. For starters, gross margin guidance fell to 72% from nearly 75% this quarter. On $130 billion of revenue, three points of margin is roughly $4 billion of gross profit. Rising memory costs are the likely culprit. Further, long-term debt climbed to $32.4 billion from $7.5 billion at fiscal year-end, meaning Nvidia is now borrowing while it repurchases stock and finances its customers. Lastly, and most importantly, the company has no permanent chief executive, and an independent board committee investigation remains open with a wide range of potential outcomes, some of which can be problematic for the company.

Here is what we find most telling. CoreWeave rose about 5.4% and Nebius about 7%, both outpacing Nvidia itself. They are very beaten up, but it’s a vote of confidence that one of their key financiers (NVDA) will continue to provide financing.

Buy And Forget? It’s Not That Easy

Buy an S&P 500 index fund, set up automatic contributions, and forget about it. It’s one of the most common pieces of retirement advice, and the chart below makes a strong case for it. In January 1940, the S&P 500, as reconstructed by Robert Shiller, stood at about 12. Today, it’s around 7,500. World War II, regional wars, recessions, oil shocks, a pandemic, and a long list of financial crises look like minor speed bumps. For anyone saving for retirement, the answer seems obvious: why do anything other than buy and forget?

Unfortunately, it’s not that easy. The chart shows what the market did over 86 years. It doesn’t show what happened to investors who depended on it during the 20 or 30 years that mattered most to them.

Potential signal:

  • I am selling gold.

  • I am looking for continuation to the downside for a move to $3550.

  • I am setting a stop loss just above $3850.

Gold has now broken yet another support level on Wednesday, as we continue to see real rates punish gold holders.

Gold

The gold market has collapsed during the trading session yet again, as we are now well below the $3,850 level, an area that I had watched previously. Now that we're below there, it looks like we've probably seen more FOMO shorting into the market.

The question is what's going on? The biggest problem is going to be real rates at the moment. Real rates in America and several other countries, for that matter, pay you to hold on to government debt. So the question for most professional managers will be: why bother risking your account in the gold market when you can simply earn a return for owning government debt, and it's guaranteed?

With this being the case, it makes a certain amount of sense that gold sells off.

If inflation drops, those bonds become even more valuable, as they will pay the same rate with inflation dropping. So the real rate only gets bigger. With this being the case, it makes a certain amount of sense that gold sells off.

Now we're looking for major support levels underneath to perhaps try to find value. That would be somewhere closer to the $3,500 level. In other words, I think we have further to the downside.

All things being equal, though, this is a market that could bounce occasionally. Those bounces, for me, end up being selling opportunities. I have no interest in buying gold in the current environment at this moment. I do think gold eventually turns around, but we're not there yet.

From a technical analysis standpoint, you can see that on the charts. The $3,500 level was an important level. If we turn around and rally from here, it's really not until we clear the $4,000 level that you can have any real conversation of perhaps going bullish, the trend changing, whatever.

I think at this point in time, anytime you get a rally, you're a seller. Or I think some people are probably just selling now and aiming for that breakdown.

Bank of America Fund Manager Survey Update

On Tuesday, we put out a summary of the monthly Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey. This month, they surveyed 169 institutional managers with ~$461B in AUM:

Here were the 5 key points:

1) Fund managers piled back into the consumer in November, with combined allocation to discretionary + staples jumping 28 ppts to a net 38% underweight from a net 66% underweight last month, the biggest monthly increase since June 2006. Discretionary moved to a net 20% underweight from a net 34% underweight, while staples climbed to a net 18% underweight from a net 32% underweight. We have spent months pounding the table on buying anything with a fork or a sneaker (restaurants, apparel, footwear, etc.), with opinion now following trend. Even after the rotation, discretionary still sits 0.8 standard deviations below its long-term average and staples 1.0 standard deviations below, leaving plenty of room to work higher.

2) Fund managers cut their technology allocation by 25 ppts to a net 12% overweight from a net 37% overweight last month, the biggest monthly reduction since June 2006, leaving positioning 0.5 standard deviations below its long-term average. The cut comes just one month after managers piled into their most overweight tech position since August 2020, with everyone swept up in the AI trade just in time for it to roll over.

3) Inflation expectations have inflected lower, with a net 32% of fund managers now expecting lower global CPI in 12 months’ time (vs. net 5% last month), the lowest inflation expectations since October 2024. Fears of a second wave of inflation have faded along with them, slipping to just 14% as a tail risk.

4) A majority of fund managers (52%) now expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut over the next six months, up from 30% last month and just 14% in September, while those expecting no cuts fell to 40%. The message to hyperscalers is clear, with a record net 38% saying companies are overinvesting and just 16% wanting them to boost capex (the lowest since May 2020), while AI hyperscaler bonds remain the most likely source of a systemic credit event (38%).

5) “Long global semiconductors” remains the most crowded trade at 39%, though that share has fallen steadily from a record 82% in July 2026. Behind it, “short China stocks” has popped up as the second most crowded trade at 14%, a consensus we are happy to take the other side of. We continue to see China as the cheapest way to play AI globally, with BABA effectively serving as a Chinese AI ETF while also acting as a toll taker on the Chinese consumer recovery.

Advance Auto Parts Update

For newer readers, here’s a quick overview of the key drivers behind our thesis on Advance Auto Parts, the long-neglected auto parts retailer undergoing a back-to-basics turnaround with substantial margin recovery still ahead:

Company Overview

  • Leading automotive aftermarket parts retailer founded in 1929; headquartered in Raleigh, NC

  • Blended-box model serving Pro (~50% of sales) and DIY (~50%) from the same locations

  • 4,087 Advance Auto Parts stores + 238 Carquest stores as of Q3 2026 (4,325 total); #3 U.S. player behind O’Reilly and AutoZone

  • Also services 787 independently owned Carquest branded stores across the US, Canada, Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, and various Caribbean islands

  • 90% of sales from maintenance and break-fix categories

  • Net sales from continuing operations ~$8.6B in FY2025

  • Revenue mix: parts and batteries 63%, accessories and chemicals 22%, engine maintenance 14%

  • Structural tailwinds: average U.S. vehicle age at a record 12.8 years in 2025 (estimated 13.0 years in 2026), growing vehicle base, and rising miles traveled supporting steady 3.5%+ industry growth (DIFM outpacing DIY)

  • U.S. light-duty vehicle parc of 289M today, up from 263M in 2016 and projected to exceed 301M by 2029

  • More than 110M vehicles now sit in the prime aftermarket service window of 6 to 14 years, nearly 38% of the fleet, with S&P Global expecting that share to reach ~40% by 2028

  • Total vehicle miles traveled rebounded to 3.34T after troughing in 2021

  • $160B TAM with AAP holding just over 5% share; the big 3 hold under 30% of the industry, leaving plenty of share to be gained

  • Shares still down >80% from 2022 highs (~$240), trading at 2010 levels

Management

  • CEO Shane O’Kelly (since August 2023): proven supply chain and operations leader with 30+ years in distribution and logistics

  • Former CEO of HD Supply ($8B+ business sold to Home Depot), CEO of PetroChoice (world’s largest lubricant distributor), and 7-year U.S. Army officer

  • CFO Ryan Grimsland (late 2023): ~17 years at Lowe’s

  • Board additions: Tom Seboldt (30+ years at O’Reilly), Gregory Smith (Goodyear operations, Walmart supply chain), Brett Windom (former Pep Boys CEO)

WorldPac Sale

  • Sold WorldPac wholesale/import parts business to Carlyle for $1.5B cash (announced August 2024, closed November 2024)

  • Net proceeds ~$1.45B after taxes and fees; tax liability came in ~$200M lower than expected

  • Proceeds used for debt reduction: transformed $1.3B net debt (end-2023) into ~$80M net cash by end-2024

  • Leverage taken down from >4x to 2.2x at end of Q3 2026 (within target range of 2x to 2.5x), vs. 2.1x in Q2 2026

  • $3.1B of cash on the balance sheet against $3.4B of debt at end of Q3 2026 ($349M of 1.75% notes due October 2027 now current)

  • Repurchased and retired ~$30M of principal on the 2028 senior notes in Q2 2026, the first debt reduction since the WorldPac paydown; Moody’s and S&P both moved to a stable outlook during the quarter (investment grade remains 3 notches away at Moody’s, 2 at S&P)

  • Removes lower-margin wholesale drag; simplifies focus on core retail/Pro blended-box model with solvency risk off the table

Margin Expansion

  • Operating margins bottomed in FY2024 at just 0.4% of net sales, the weakest in 20+ years due to prior expansion missteps, supply chain inefficiencies, and under-investment in core operations

  • Trailing peers dramatically: AutoZone/O’Reilly at ~19-20%; AAP historically maintained 9-11% before missteps

  • Productivity review identifies >500 bps of margin opportunity

  • FY2025 adjusted operating margin of 2.5% (+213 bps Y/Y from near-breakeven)

  • Q3 2026 adjusted operating margin of 4.5% (+10 bps Y/Y) on a negative comp, with adjusted operating income of $91M ahead of consensus $88.4M; excluding Q2 tariff refunds, one of the strongest margin quarters since the strategic plan began; YTD adjusted operating margin of 4.6% vs. 2.2% last year

  • Q3 2026 adjusted gross margin of 44.7% (-16 bps Y/Y) on ~40 bps of DIY mix, fuel, and supply chain deleverage plus ~20 bps of product mix into motor oil, partially offset by ~40 bps of net LIFO benefit; YTD 45.3% (+150 bps Y/Y), with merchandising initiatives contributing ~100 bps of gross margin expansion YTD

  • Not yet fully passing commodity cost inflation through to customers, viewing much of the pressure as transitory; rational fast follower on pricing, not leading the market higher or lower

  • Q3 2026 adjusted SG&A of 40.2% of net sales, 26 bps of leverage Y/Y with dollars down ~2%; productivity found in non-customer-facing areas (indirect spend, cloud consolidation) reinvested in the frontline

  • FY2026 guidance: adjusted operating margin narrowed to 4.0-4.3% from 3.8-4.5% (4.15% midpoint reaffirmed, +150+ bps)

  • Management expects at least another 100+ bps expansion in FY2027, a third straight year of 100+ bps expansion, driven by merchandising, labor productivity, and supply chain (incl. 20+ bps from transportation); built off the H2 2026 base (~3.65%) rather than the full year given ~30 bps of non-repeating tariff refunds and ~50 bps of fuel/deleverage pressure lingering into H1 2027, implying ~4.7%

  • SG&A expected to grow roughly in line with sales in FY2027 as productivity savings are reinvested in stores, hubs, and frontline labor, leaving gross margin as the main driver of incremental expansion

  • Medium-term target: 7% adjusted operating margin still viewed as appropriate, though pushed out as the original plan assumed steady low-single-digit comps; implies ~$630M operating income on $9B sales

Q3 Commentary

Advance’s third quarter was a tale of two halves, with a sluggish start giving way to improving trends and stronger execution across the business. Comp sales declined 1.2%, missing consensus expectations for a 0.4% increase and decelerating from Q2’s -0.5%, while revenue of $2.01B came in ~$30M below the Street. Profitability held up better, with adjusted operating income of $91M ahead of the $88.4M consensus estimate as adjusted operating margins expanded 10 bps Y/Y to 4.5%. Most importantly, management raised its full-year free cash flow guidance by 50% to ~$150M, an improvement of more than $400M Y/Y that will mark Advance’s first full year of positive free cash flow since FY2022.

The weakness in the headline comp was largely a function of where the quarter started. The low point came in the final four weeks of Q2, which ended in mid-July, when comps declined ~3% on a nearly 7% drop in DIY, which management described as the channel’s weakest stretch of the year. From there, trends steadily improved, with comps down ~2% through the first eight weeks of Q3 before turning positive in the final four weeks as DIY declines narrowed to the low single digits. That momentum has carried into Q4, with Pro sales growing at a low-to-mid single-digit rate in the early weeks of the quarter, while management’s full-year comp guidance of ~1% implies further acceleration in overall comps.

That acceleration in Pro continues a trend that has been the steadiest part of the business all year. The channel, which accounts for ~half of sales, grew at a low-single-digit rate in Q3, remained positive every month, and reached ~3% growth in the final four weeks. Main Street Pro, the local two- or three-bay shops that account for ~80% of Pro sales and carry better margins, outpaced the overall channel by ~100 bps, driven by new customer wins and existing accounts moving into higher weekly spending tiers. That is the payoff from better parts availability and consistently getting deliveries out in under 40 minutes.

Keep in mind that reported Pro growth continues to understate the underlying strength, as management deliberately walks away from lower-margin national accounts to concentrate on Main Street. This self-imposed headwind weighed ~100 bps on Pro growth in the quarter (~50 bps on total sales). With that headwind set to roll off by early Q1, reported Pro growth should accelerate in 2027 even before accounting for any further improvement in the business.

DIY, the other half of the business, has been the harder fight. It’s no secret that Advance caters to the lower- and middle-income consumer, and with DIY accounting for ~half of sales, pressure on that customer is hard to miss in the comp. That matters for margins as well as sales, as DIY is Advance’s highest-margin channel, meaning any recovery would bring a mix tailwind alongside it. The channel declined at a low-single-digit rate in Q3, yet nearly every metric tied to O’Kelly’s initiatives continued to move in the right direction. Better training, service, and in-store execution pushed Net Promoter Scores above 80 from the high 70s last quarter, while in-store attachment rates climbed to the mid-30% range from ~30% and DIY units per transaction grew at a low-single-digit rate, driving average ticket growth above same-SKU inflation.

Management is pulling every internal lever available, from the Advance Rewards loyalty program, paid search optimization, and sharper value messaging to the ARGOS private label for customers trading down. Meanwhile, ReliaScan, a free check-engine diagnostic tool, rolled out across most stores during the quarter, and Zebra devices in every store are shifting team member hours from back-room tasks to selling. These encouraging signs tell us that Advance’s internal initiatives are working and translating into better results when customers come through the door. The next step is getting more customers through it.

That is where the macro backdrop is finally starting to turn in Advance’s favor. Much of the pressure on its core customer this year has come down to pain at the pump, with energy accounting for 17.4% of pre-tax income for the bottom 20% of earners, the bulk of which is gasoline, versus just 2.7% for the top quintile.

Gas prices rolled over in late September and have been falling steadily since, dropping ~$0.75 a gallon from the peak to a national average of $3.75, an eight-month low, with RBOB gasoline futures now below $2.50, pointing to more relief ahead.

The spending data responded almost exactly as you would expect. BofA data show lower-income households posted the strongest total card spending growth of any group in October at +5.9%, while holiday spending by lower-income households, which trailed every other cohort in October of both 2024 and 2025, is now up ~9% Y/Y. Broader October retail sales confirmed the strength, rising 6.8% Y/Y for the strongest annual gain since October 2022.

Source: ZeroHedge

Lower gas prices will continue to bring inflation expectations down, which goes hand in hand with consumer sentiment, as seen below:

Less pain at the pump points to a lift in sentiment from today’s washed-out levels, with the UMich index at 48 in October, within a stone’s throw of May’s reading of 44.8. If May does ultimately prove to be the trough, the historical data is encouraging: following the last nine sentiment troughs, the S&P 500 delivered an average 12-month return of 24.1%. The point is, these are the times to be BUYERS of beaten-down consumer names, not SELLERS.

Beyond the consumer backdrop, ~90% of what Advance sells is tied to maintenance and break/fix needs. Q3 strength came from maintenance and failure categories like motor oil, batteries, and wipers, while hard parts remained weak as customers put off larger repairs. But deferred maintenance can only be kicked down the road for so long. The average age of U.S. light vehicles reached a record 12.8 years in 2025 and is expected to hit 13.0 years this year, with more than 110M vehicles now sitting in the prime aftermarket service window of 6 to 14 years. That represents nearly 38% of the fleet, a share S&P Global expects to reach ~40% by 2028.

In the meantime, management continues to control what it can, with the supply chain remaining the centerpiece of that effort. The distribution network has been consolidated from nearly 40 facilities running multiple systems to 15 operating on a single warehouse management platform, with process improvements rolling through each DC in stages through mid-2027 to lower handling costs, improve shipment accuracy, and shorten lead times. Carrier contracts have also been rebid, consolidating volume across 70% fewer carriers for 20+ bps of cost savings, even in a flattish sales environment.

The market hub network, modeled on the hub-and-spoke system that best-in-class peers have used for years, reached 46 locations following 13 openings YTD, with 70%+ of stores set to sit inside a hub ecosystem by year end and ~60 hubs expected to serve the majority of the store base by mid-2027. Each hub carries ~85,000 SKUs for same-day availability, with hub markets historically delivering ~100 bps of comp lift.

These self-help initiatives across the supply chain, merchandising, and stores have already driven significant margin improvement with very little help from the top line. Advance delivered a 4.5% adjusted operating margin in Q3 despite a negative comp, with SG&A dollars down ~2% Y/Y. Management noted that, excluding the tariff refunds received last quarter, it was one of the strongest margin quarters since the strategic plan began two years ago. Zooming out, adjusted operating margins have climbed from a trough of 0.4% in FY2024, the weakest level in more than 20 years, to 2.5% in FY2025 and ~4.15% at the midpoint of FY2026 guidance. That progress has come alongside comp growth of just 0.8% last year and ~1% this year.

For 2027, management continues to expect at least another 100 bps of margin expansion, but guided investors to build off the second half of this year rather than the full year, given ~30 bps of tariff refunds that won’t repeat and fuel and deleveraging pressures likely to linger into the first half. That puts next year’s adjusted operating margin at ~4.7%, driven by merchandising initiatives, labor productivity, and supply chain savings, including 20+ bps from transportation.

More consistent comp growth remains the missing piece of the turnaround and the key to unlocking Advance’s longer-term margin potential. The original roadmap assumed steady low-single-digit comp growth, which has been slow to materialize, pushing out the timeline to management’s still-intact medium-term operating margin target of 7%. The good news is that, with its national account headwind behind it and a stronger Pro business, alongside even a modest recovery in DIY traffic, Advance has what we believe is its strongest top-line setup since the turnaround began.

At a 7% margin on ~$9B of revenue, Advance would generate ~$630M of operating income, a level we believe supports close to $7 per share in normalized earnings power, more than double the current run rate. For context, Advance generated 9% to 11% operating margins before the missteps that derailed the business, while O’Reilly and AutoZone operate at 18% to 20% today, leaving plenty of room to close the gap.

Meanwhile, the importance of the free cash flow inflection can’t be overstated. YTD free cash flow sits at +$109M versus an outflow of $277M last year, with the raised ~$150M full-year target coming even as capex steps up to ~$300M to fund new market hubs, new stores, store upgrades, and in-store technology. Management expects free cash flow to improve again in 2027, even with capex at or above this year’s level. That cash gives Advance the flexibility to keep investing in growth while chipping away at its debt, supporting the goal of returning to investment grade and eventually resuming share buybacks.

While the market has grown impatient waiting for the turnaround to move faster, we believe it underappreciates how much of the foundation has been rebuilt over the past few years and the upside that creates. At just 12.7x forward earnings, the bar is low enough that modest top-line improvement and consistent execution will be enough to move the stock. With much of the heavy lifting behind it and the road ahead starting to clear, Advance looks well positioned for a stronger 2027.

  • Received the vast majority of IEEPA tariff refunds applied for. Refunds pulling forward $70-80M of growth investment planned for 2027, with SG&A expected back to ~23% of sales in 2027

  • On track to reach at-or-above industry-average USMCA-qualified import mix (up from ~1/3 at program start) and reducing China-sourced U.S. sales to <5% by end-2026 (from ~20%), both ahead of plan

  • 2H’26 margin expansion is expected to lean meaningfully on tariff mitigation, specifically continued USMCA compliance progress and shifting U.S. tools production from China to North America

Deleveraging Through Asset Sales & Capital Allocation

  • Debt reduced >$3.7B since FY2022; net leverage improved from 5.9x (end-FY2023) to 3.4x (end-FY2025); on track for ~2.5x by end-FY2026 inclusive of buybacks

  • Convergent Security Solutions sold July 2022 for net proceeds of $3.1B

  • Mechanical Solutions business sold July 2022 for net proceeds of $916M

  • Oil and Gas business sold August 2022

  • Infrastructure business sold April 2024 for net proceeds of $729M

  • CAM sold to Howmet Aerospace on April 6, 2026 for $1.8B all-cash (18x EBITDA, above the $1.0-1.5B expectation), ahead of the prior H1 2026 timeline; ~$1.8B of proceeds received net of cash sold, with a $273.7M pre-tax gain ($1.08 of GAAP EPS)

  • ~$1.7B of debt reduction executed in 2Q using CAM proceeds plus operating cash flow

  • Over $6.3B in cumulative asset sales over ~4 years; multi-year restructuring now complete – focus shifts to share repurchases

  • Management considers large structural portfolio moves finished (“end of the major transformational cycle”). The Excel (Hustler large-format mowers, ~$300M of revenue) divestiture announced in September was pruning, since SWK could already cover the outdoor zero-turn professional gas market with Cub Cadet, with closing expected ~year-end.

  • Completed the $500M repurchase authorization with ~2.5M shares repurchased for $250M in 3Q (~5.8M shares total). Board approved a new $1B authorization on Oct 29 (expires Oct 2029); capital allocation now biased toward buybacks while the M&A pipeline builds

  • Any future M&A would be tools brands or technologies that accelerate the organic story in target verticals. Management explicitly ruled out diversifying acquisitions or adding another leg of the stool

  • 3Q’26 balance sheet: cash ~$0.7B, long-term debt $4.7B, no short-term borrowings, ~$3.7B of total additional liquidity, next debt maturity in 2028

Return to Growth

  • Stabilizing after multiyear pressures; FY2025 organic sales -1%; 2026 organic sales accelerating each quarter (Q1 flat, Q2 +3%, Q3 +4%)

  • Q3 2026 revenue $3.73B (+4% organic), at the top of the +3-4% organic guide

  • 2026 guidance: low single-digit organic growth (total revenue ~flat on CAM close and gas walk-behind licensing). Tools & Outdoor LSD organic growth driven by share gains in a ~flat to down market

  • Q3 2026 standouts: Power tools organic +10% (up from +8% in Q2), U.S. retail up mid-single digits, U.S. C&I channel up mid-teens (accelerating from low double digits in Q2), all three priority brands (DEWALT, STANLEY, CRAFTSMAN) growing organically for a second straight quarter

  • Reworked 2026 promotional construct (e.g., which free tool is bundled with a battery purchase) based on nationwide A/B testing, driving accretive volume growth in higher-margin products despite a heavier promotional environment across the industry

  • Industrial fasteners organic +10%; Outdoor organic -12% on weather in the U.S. plus Automotive organic -2% on OEM caution the drags

  • Underlying demand is flattish overall. Commercial and industrial professional is very strong, housing has not inflected, and the DIY consumer is stabilized rather than growing

  • STANLEY generated positive organic growth in each of the past 2 quarters, on pace with the mid-2026 target; management still points to 2H’26 for consistent STANLEY performance. 2 of 8 product refresh waves complete, with wave 3 underway.

  • Over 60% of STANLEY is European, sold through wholesalers, where SWK previously had no dedicated sales force. Those resources are now in place and producing growth

  • CRAFTSMAN also positive organically in Q2 and Q3, with the relaunch (most new product launches since SWK acquired the brand in 2017) and new V20 advanced batteries driving momentum alongside record brand engagement; management targets consistent performance into 2027.

  • Growth led by DEWALT ($7B+ franchise, ~half of total revenue, low-single-digit growth in FY2025, organic growth across all regions in Q3) alongside the long-awaited inflection in CRAFTSMAN and STANLEY.

  • The DEWALT push expands from traditional residential and carpentry strength into commercial and industrial mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and concrete

  • Battery ecosystem builds a moat: users are >80% predisposed to stay in their current battery platform on the next purchase. SWK competes on battery performance (20V, the industry-exclusive FLEXVOLT 20V/60V, larger-format packs moving gas-powered concrete work to battery) plus full workflows for each trade down to specialty tools, with room to win specialty share of wallet from smaller players

  • Management’s pricing argument on DEWALT: large professional enterprise users are relatively price insensitive because what is sold is labor arbitrage. Turning a two-person job into a one-person job matters on a data center timeline measured in hours and days

  • Management expects consistent, repeatable growth across all three brands by the middle of next year

  • U.S. C&I channel expected to approach ~10% of total Tools & Outdoor sales in 2026 on ~double-digit organic growth; projects served by this channel represent trillions of dollars of committed capital spending over the next 5 years (data centers, power generation, prefab manufacturing).

  • Management views this as more than a data center trade, with new tradespeople entering the workforce needing to be outfitted and a backlog of other construction work behind data centers

  • Long-term goal: mid-single-digit organic growth (2-3x market/GDP in normalized environments)

  • ~50% of Tools & Outdoor tied to residential construction: 27% new construction, 23% repair/remodel

  • Key secular drivers: housing construction recovery, lower rates tailwind, U.S. housing shortage of ~4M homes, significantly aged housing stock (>42 years)

  • 13.9M homes owned by Baby Boomers and the Silent Generation expected to return to the market from 2026-2036, a 33.7% (3.5M) increase over the prior decade’s pace

  • Innovation cycle time improved 30% by the end of this year, feeding a product pipeline across DEWALT, STANLEY, and CRAFTSMAN

  • Introduced the world’s first downward drilling, fleet-capable robot accelerating data center construction (80 weeks saved across 10 projects, 99.97% accuracy)

Key Financials + Valuation

  • FY2025: Net sales $15.1B (-2% Y/Y, -1% organic); adj. EPS $4.67 (+7% Y/Y); FCF $688M (ahead of prior ~$600M guide)

  • YTD’26: Net sales $11.54B (+0.8% Y/Y); adj. EPS $4.66 (vs. $3.26 LY); FCF $836M (vs. -$195M LY)

  • 2026 guidance: adj. EPS $5.95-6.25 (midpoint $6.10, +31% Y/Y), including ~$0.60 from net tariff refunds and excluding any potential Q4 refunds; FCF $1.0-1.2B; organic sales low single digits; ~350 bps adj. gross margin expansion including ~150 bps from refunds

  • 4Q’26 guide: net sales ~$3.6B (flat reported), organic +2-4%, adj. EPS ~$1.45 (including ~$0.25 of refund-related costs and taxes)

  • Dividend: quarterly rate now $0.84 (from $0.83); ~3% yield; 149 consecutive years of payments (longest streak of any industrial company on the NYSE); 58 consecutive years of increases (every year since 1968)

Q3 Commentary

For a company the market has long treated as a housing proxy, Stanley Black & Decker keeps finding ways to grow without any help from housing. Organic growth accelerated to 4% in Q3 on revenue of $3.73B, landing at the high end of guidance and marking the fastest pace since Q4 2021. Adjusted EPS of $2.31 and adjusted gross margin of 39.4% both benefited from IEEPA tariff refunds, which generated a $180.7M pretax gain in the quarter, worth ~$0.67 of EPS and ~430 bps of margin. Backing out the tariff benefit, the underlying results were every bit as strong. Adjusted EPS of ~$1.64 (+14.7% Y/Y) still topped the ~$1.56 consensus and the high end of guidance, while adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% cleared the long-awaited 35% threshold at the heart of the entire turnaround. That prompted management to raise FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.95-$6.25 (+31% Y/Y at the midpoint) and its free cash flow outlook to $1.0-$1.2B (vs. $688M in FY25), with the underlying operational outlook unchanged.

We laid out the full thesis last month (see article below), walking through how SWK has pulled its own levers to grow and expand margins while housing remains in the gutter.

Little has changed since then. Housing remains under pressure, with management still planning around a flat-to-down tools market, yet SWK continues to take share through its own execution. That progress was well underway before the tariff refunds arrived, but the refunds have given the strategy a shot in the arm. Rather than let them flow straight to the bottom line, management is directing the bulk toward growth investments on top of the $75-100M already planned for 2026. In effect, it is pulling forward $70-80M of spending originally earmarked for 2027 to expand its field presence, step up digital marketing and brand activation, while accelerating new product innovation.

Those investments continue to gain traction, with organic growth climbing from flat in Q1 to +3% in Q2 and +4% in Q3. That puts FY26 on track to be SWK’s first year of positive organic growth since the pandemic-driven pull-forward in 2021.

Power tools once again did the heavy lifting in Q3, accelerating to +10% organic growth from +8% in Q2, which had already marked the category’s strongest growth in several years. Much of that strength traces back to the pro customer. The U.S. commercial and industrial channel accelerated to mid-teens growth from low double digits last quarter as data center construction and a broad backlog of other job site work keep pro demand running hot, a trend management expects to continue. U.S. retail added mid-single-digit growth of its own, a solid result given how long the DIY customer has been under pressure.

Most encouraging is how broad the growth has become. For years, DEWALT was left to carry the portfolio on its own, but STANLEY and CRAFTSMAN have now joined it, with all three brands delivering organic growth for two consecutive quarters. That consistency is a direct result of one of the biggest changes under CEO Chris Nelson, who reorganized the company around its brands rather than individual product lines, giving each its own general manager and a clearly defined end user.

Built for the pro, DEWALT grew across every region as investments in end-user specialists embedded with each trade continue to pay off. Those efforts are pulling more pros into a battery ecosystem where more than 80% of users stick with the same platform on their next purchase. CRAFTSMAN, repositioned as SWK’s DIY brand, is in its most active launch year since being acquired in 2017. Influencer partnerships are driving record brand engagement, while a ~30% reduction in new product development time across the company, with platforming serving as a major productivity unlock, is helping bring new tools to market faster. STANLEY, which generates more than 60% of its sales in Europe, is working through an eight-wave refresh of its product lines, now supported by a dedicated sales force focused on the European hand tool wholesalers that drive the business.

Management expects that momentum to carry into the fourth quarter, guiding to +3-4% organic growth in Tools & Outdoor and keeping the segment on track for low-single-digit organic growth for the full year.

Home Depot and Lowe’s both reported results this week for quarters that ran about a month past SWK’s quarter-end, offering a positive early read on Q4. Home Depot (15% of sales) beat expectations with its highest comp growth in four years, led by double-digit comps in its power tools department, while its Pro customer continued to outpace DIY. Lowe’s (12% of sales) also beat, with comps up 1.8% on positive growth in tools and hardware. It also cited strong Pro demand for new DEWALT generators and an expanded lineup that now gives it the largest DEWALT assortment of any U.S. home improvement retailer. Both retailers raised full-year sales guidance on steady underlying demand, with SWK’s brands front and center heading into the key holiday selling season.

The progress on adjusted gross margin has been just as impressive. Excluding refunds, adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% expanded 350 bps Y/Y on productivity and favorable mix, up from ~31.2% in Q2 and more than 15 ppts above the 19.5% trough in Q4 2022. Including refunds, YTD adjusted gross margin now stands at 34.4% (+460 bps Y/Y), keeping FY26 on track for ~34.2% (~350 bps of expansion, ~150 bps from refunds).

Even as that refund benefit falls away, management expects to land at or very close to 35% in 2027, with another 150-200 bps of net productivity gains and a modest low-single-digit price increase offsetting rising inflation. That keeps the long-awaited 35-37% target for 2028 firmly in place. For context, the last time SWK cleared 35% for a full year was 2018, when it earned $8.15 per share and the stock traded north of $150. With a far leaner cost structure today and a shrinking share count, we see a path not only back to those earnings levels, but considerably beyond over time.

That margin progress is translating just as clearly into free cash flow. Q3 free cash flow of $585M came in well ahead of the ~$222M the Street was expecting, bringing YTD free cash flow to $836M versus an outflow of $195M a year ago. At the $1.1B midpoint of FY26 guidance, backing out ~$300M of tariff refunds and adding back ~$200M of one-time taxes and fees tied to the CAM sale leaves ~$1.0B of underlying free cash flow, or a ~6.2% yield at today’s price.

With leverage heading toward ~2.5x by year-end and balance sheet repair now a closed chapter, that cash is making its way back to shareholders. SWK repurchased $500M of stock this year, retiring ~4% of its shares, before the Board approved a new $1B authorization in October. That comes alongside a ~3.0% dividend yield and a payout history spanning 150 consecutive years, with 59 straight annual increases, the longest such record of any industrial company on the NYSE.

With the stock up 54% YTD and more than double its lows, the market has clearly started to reward SWK for its execution. Shares now trade at ~17x forward earnings, in line with their historical average, so a breather after such a big move would come as no surprise. Zooming out, however, we still see this story in its early innings. Execution alone has carried the stock this far, with the housing tailwind still ahead. A ~4M-unit housing shortage, an average home now ~42 years old, and millennials moving into their prime family formation years all point to a recovery being a matter of when, not if. From today’s depressed levels, we continue to see the risk-reward in housing as firmly skewed to the upside. When housing finally turns, it will be the whipped cream and cherry on top of an already improving business.

Q3 Earnings Breakdown

10 Key Points

1) SWK reported Q3 revenue of $3.73B, down 0.6% Y/Y on a reported basis and up 4% organically. The figure was in line with consensus and at the top end of the 3% to 4% organic growth guide. Higher volume (+6%) was offset by lower pricing (-2%) and a ~4% portfolio drag from the CAM divestiture and the transition to a licensing model for gas walk-behind outdoor products, with currency flat. Organic growth accelerated from flat in Q1 and +3% in Q2 to its highest quarterly level since 2021. Volume strength was concentrated in U.S. retail (up mid-single digits) and the commercial and industrial (C&I) channel (up mid-teens) within Tools & Outdoor. YTD revenue reached $11.54B (+0.8% Y/Y), with YTD organic growth of ~2%.

2) Adjusted EPS of $2.31 came in well ahead of consensus of ~$1.56 and $0.76 above the midpoint of July guidance, up 61.5% Y/Y from $1.43. The outperformance was driven primarily by net tariff refunds (~$0.67 after related incentive compensation, growth investments, and taxes), along with ~$0.02 each from a lower share count and lower net interest expense. Excluding refunds, adjusted EPS of ~$1.64 (+14.7% Y/Y) still cleared both consensus and the high end of the $1.50 to $1.60 guide. YTD adjusted EPS reached $4.66 versus $3.26 last year (+42.9%).

3) Adjusted gross margin reached 39.4% in Q3, up 780 bps Y/Y, with ~430 bps coming from net tariff refunds. Even excluding refunds, adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% (+350 bps Y/Y) topped consensus of ~34.3%, clearing the 35% threshold on net productivity gains and favorable product mix. That compares to ~31.2% ex-refunds in Q2, bringing YTD adjusted gross margin to 34.4% (+460 bps Y/Y). For the full year, management now expects ~350 bps of expansion off FY25’s 30.7%, including ~150 bps from net tariff refunds. Q4 remains guided to 34% to 35% (vs. 33.3% last year) on continued productivity and tariff mitigation initiatives, with the long-term target of above 35% toward 37% unchanged.

4) The Tools & Outdoor segment posted Q3 net sales of $3.34B, up 2% on a reported basis and 4% organically. Higher volume (+7%) was partially offset by lower pricing (-3%) and a 2% drag from the gas walk-behind licensing transition, with currency flat. Management noted that lower pricing reflects the promotional calendar reset running to plan, with list prices holding. Growth was led by power tools, where organic growth accelerated to +10% from +8% in Q2, alongside a 2% gain in hand tools, accessories, and storage, partially offset by a 12% decline in Outdoor on weather pressure. North America grew 6% organically on U.S. retail up mid-single digits and C&I up mid-teens. Europe grew 1%, while Rest of World declined 1% on softer Latin America, bringing YTD segment organic growth to ~2%. Adjusted segment margin of 17.6% expanded 560 bps Y/Y, with ~430 bps from net tariff refunds and the balance from net productivity and favorable mix. Management still expects low-single-digit organic growth for the segment in FY26, driven by share gains in a ~flat to down market.

5) The Engineered Fastening segment (~11% of total sales) posted Q3 net sales of $396M, down 21% on a reported basis but up 2% organically. The CAM divestiture created a 22% headwind, partially offset by volume (+1%) and pricing (+1%), with currency down 1%. Industrial grew 10% organically on project-driven wins and solid commercial execution, more than offsetting a 2% decline in Automotive as OEM customers grew more cautious on launches, production schedules, and capital deployment. Adjusted segment margin of 11.7% declined 110 bps Y/Y on automotive demand pressure, with the segment receiving no tariff refund benefit. YTD segment organic growth stands at ~4%, helped by aerospace strength in Q1 before the CAM sale. Given the deterioration in auto, management lowered its FY26 outlook to low-single-digit organic growth (from low-to-mid single digits), with a flat Y/Y segment margin (previously positive).

6) Cash from operating activities of $659M drove free cash flow of $585M in the quarter, up 276.7% from $155M last year and well ahead of consensus of ~$222M. Performance was supported by both operational cash generation and net tariff refunds, alongside disciplined working capital management, with inventories down to $3.84B from $4.16B at year-end. YTD free cash flow reached $836M versus an outflow of $195M a year ago, already well above FY25’s $688M. Management raised FY26 FCF guidance by $400M at the midpoint to $1.0B to $1.2B (from $600M to $800M), versus consensus of ~$775M. The new range incorporates YTD outperformance and refunds received, net of projected CAM-related taxes and fees.

7) SWK repurchased ~2.5M shares for $250M in Q3, fully utilizing the $500M authorization approved in April (~5.8M shares repurchased in total), with diluted share count down 2.2% Y/Y to ~148.6M. The Board followed with a new $1B repurchase authorization on October 29, running through October 2029. With management describing the company as being at the end of its major transformational cycle and any future portfolio moves limited to pruning around the edges, capital allocation priorities now center on funding organic growth, returning capital to shareholders, and bolt-on M&A when appropriate. On the dividend front, the quarterly payout stands at $0.84 per share (~3% yield), extending a record of 150 consecutive years of payments, alongside 59 consecutive years of increases.

8) SWK ended Q3 with $741M of cash (up from $280M at year-end) against $4.7B of long-term debt, with short-term borrowings fully paid down from $606M at year-end. Total liquidity stands at ~$3.7B, with no debt maturities until 2028. The lower debt load and strong YTD cash generation have also brought the full-year net interest expense estimate down to ~$250M from ~$255M. Management remains on track for net debt to adjusted EBITDA of ~2.5x by year-end, inclusive of buybacks, down from 5.9x at the end of 2023, with maintaining an investment-grade credit rating a stated priority.

9) SWK has now received the vast majority of the IEEPA tariff refunds it applied for, recognizing a $180.7M pretax gain in Q3 ($298.7M YTD), with FY26 adjusted EPS guidance including ~$0.60 of net refund benefit. Rather than letting the refunds fall to the bottom line, management is using them to pull forward $70M to $80M of growth investment originally planned for 2027 across field presence, brand activation, and the new product pipeline. That lifts FY26 SG&A to ~23.5% to 24% of sales (including ~80 bps of refund-related costs) before returning toward ~23% in 2027. On the cost side, the temporary period of lower tariffs since late February is still largely offsetting rising inflation in steel, electrical components, resins, battery metals, and tungsten, with tariffs assumed to return to IEEPA levels very late in the year. With inflation to address in 2027 regardless of the tariff path, management plans to pair continued productivity with a price increase likely around the turn of the year.

10) SWK raised and tightened FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.95 to $6.25 from a prior range of $5.20 to $5.80, with the $6.10 midpoint implying +31% Y/Y growth versus consensus of ~$5.60. Of the $0.60 midpoint increase, ~$0.55 reflects incremental Q3 net tariff refunds. The remaining ~$0.05 comes from a lower share count (~150M from ~151M) and below-the-line items, leaving the underlying operational outlook unchanged and excluding any potential Q4 refunds. Total revenue is still expected to be ~flat Y/Y, with low-single-digit organic growth driven by solid volume and ~flat pricing. For Q4, management guided to net sales of ~$3.6B, organic growth of 2% to 4%, and adjusted EPS of ~$1.45, including ~$0.25 of incremental costs and taxes tied to refunds already received.

data.title: Gold Continues To Hit New Yearly Lows: When Will It End?
data.description:
Gold remained under strong pressure on Thursday, trading around 3,735 USD per ounce – its lowest level since September 2025. The main negative factor for the market remains expectations of further rate hikes in the US following a series of hawkish signals from the Fed.

Minutes from the October meeting showed that a majority of FOMC members saw additional tightening as necessary to bring inflation back under control. At the meeting itself, the rate was kept in the 3.75–4.00% range by a 10–2 majority, following a 25-basis-point increase in September.

Several Fed officials have also maintained a hawkish tone. Christopher Waller again acknowledged the possibility of a 50-basis-point rate hike in December. John Williams and Alberto Musalem also made clear that the tightening cycle is probably not over yet. Markets now estimate the probability of a 25-basis-point move in December at 90%, with the chance of a 50-basis-point increase at around 10%.

At the same time, macroeconomic data are sending mixed signals but do not yet indicate a sharp economic slowdown. Retail sales rose 0.2% month-on-month in October, but industrial production unexpectedly fell 0.4%, and the NAHB housing market index dropped to 25 points, its lowest level since 2012.

Against this backdrop, the combination of factors remains unfavourable for gold: high inflation, resilient demand in the US economy and expectations of further rate hikes. Even a slight softening in the Fed’s rhetoric does not change the overall picture: high borrowing costs and a strong dollar continue to limit demand for the metal, which does not generate coupon income.

Technical Analysis

On Thursday, 19 November 2026, gold is trading around 3,724 USD on the hourly chart. On the H4 XAU/USD chart, the downtrend continues, with successively lower highs and lows. After consolidating around 3,878 USD, the price broke below the range and breached the 3,790 USD mark. The MACD signal line is below zero and pointing downwards. The expansion of the negative histogram bars indicates strengthening downward momentum. The nearest support is around 3,689 USD.

On the H1 XAU/USD chart, the price broke below the 3,753 USD level and, after a local rebound, fell below it once again. This level now acts as the nearest resistance, which the price may retest during an intraday correction. The main line of the Stochastic oscillator has dropped below the signal line, with both lines below 50 and pointing downwards. This configuration is consistent with continued pressure on the price as long as it remains below 3,753 USD.

The baseline scenario for the current session assumes a decline towards the nearest support around 3,689 USD. An hourly close below this level would open the way towards 3,608 USD, the next downside target outlined on both charts. If buyers hold support, a rebound towards 3,753 USD followed by consolidation is possible. A move above 3,753 USD would weaken the downside scenario for the day and open the way for a recovery towards 3,790 USD. The price reaction to this level will show whether the intraday correction can develop into a longer recovery following the break below the previous consolidation range on H4.

Conclusion

Gold remains under strong pressure, trading at its lowest level since September 2025, as hawkish Fed signals and expectations of further rate hikes continue to dominate the market. The October FOMC minutes confirmed that most members see additional tightening as necessary, with December rate hike probabilities at 90% for a 25-basis-point move and 10% for a 50-basis-point increase. Mixed economic data – resilient retail sales but weak industrial production and a sharp decline in housing market activity – have not yet signalled a sharp economic slowdown. For gold, the combination of high inflation, resilient demand and high borrowing costs remains unfavourable. Technically, the downtrend is intact, with support at 3,689 USD; a break below this level could open the way to 3,608 USD. A rebound towards 3,753 USD is possible if support holds, but the broader outlook remains bearish unless resistance is decisively broken.

data.title: The Power Of Compounding For Your First Ten Years Of Investing
data.description:
If you invested $100 a month in the S&P 500 (Index: SPX) for 10 years, how much would you have at the end of that time?

Five years ago, we looked at the returns an investor would accumulated after their first ten years of investing with full dividend reinvestment using historical data for the index. For it, we looked at a hypothetical series of $100 investments in the index that started in the month of June for each year from 1976 through 2011 and found what they were worth ten years later.

Five years later, we can include the outcomes of ten-year long investments that started in each June from 2012 through 2016. The following chart presents the results.

The total amount invested over ten years for each starting year is $12,000. For the forty starting years covered in this chart, we find our hypothetical investor would only have lost money for an investment that began in June 1999. That one-in-forty outcome coincides with that year's elevated stock prices, which were a consequence of the Dot-Com Bubble.

We also looked at what would happen if our hypothetical investor let the investment run. The next chart reveals how much an investment from putting $100 into the S&P 500 starting from each investment starting period covered in the first chart and going through June 2026 would be worth:

This second chart shows all our hypothetical investments starting in the Junes of 1976 through 2016 all made money and the longest running investment starting in June 1976 accumulated the most over its 50 year run. Here, our investor would have contributed a total of $60,000 into their S&P 500 investment, with the total value rising to $2,914,576 through June 2026. Of that amount, 74% (or $2,170,290) is attributable to the monthly $100 investments that were made during its first ten years.

What about the only money-losing investment over a 10-year period that began in June 1999 from the first chart? By June 2026, our hypothetical investor would have invested $32,400 in the S&P 500 index, with the total value of that investment reaching $196,850. Here, 58% (or $114,568) of that amount is attributable to the $12,000 that was invested during its first ten years.

Intrigued? To find out more about the power of compounding as it applies to an investor's first ten years of investing, check out Nick Maggiulli's 2021 article "Go Big, Then Stop".
